questions.q: In what year and location was Vitruvius's *De Architectura* rediscovered, and who found it?
questions.a: Correct: 1414, Abbey of St. Gall (Switzerland), discovered by Poggio Bracciolini. A wrong answer (e.g., "1450s, Rome, Alberti") reveals the student confuses the *rediscovery* of the text with its *first printed edition* (1486) or Alberti's *De Re Aedificatoria* (1452), missing the chronological trigger for the entire movement.

questions.q: Why did Renaissance architects treat Vitruvius as an authority rather than just an ancient curiosity?
questions.a: Correct: Vitruvius provided the *only* systematic theoretical framework linking architecture to mathematics, nature, and cosmic order—his triad (*firmitas, utilitas, venustas*) and modular proportions gave architects a "scientific" basis to claim professional status equal to painters/sculptors. A wrong answer ("they liked Roman buildings") shows the student misses the *intellectual* shift: architecture became a *discipline* governed by rules, not just a craft of copying ruins.

questions.q: Brunelleschi's dome for Florence Cathedral (1420–36) uses a double-shell structure with herringbone brickwork. Which Vitruvian principle does this innovation *most directly* embody, and why?
questions.a: Correct: *Firmitas* (structural stability). Vitruvius emphasised that materials must be used according to their nature (Book II); Brunelleschi's herringbone pattern exploits brick's tensile weakness by converting shear forces into compression, and the double shell distributes thrust—both are *applied* Vitruvian material science. A wrong answer ("Venustas because it looks beautiful") confuses aesthetic outcome with structural reasoning.

questions.q: Compare Alberti's façade of Santa Maria Novella (1456–70) with Palladio's Villa Rotonda (1566–85). How does each architect *interpret* Vitruvius's concept of *symmetria* (modular proportion) differently?
questions.a: Correct: Alberti uses *symmetria* as a *façade composition* tool—pilasters, entablatures, and scrolls organise the surface into proportional rectangles (root-2 ratios), treating the front as a painted plane. Palladio extends *symmetria* into *three-dimensional spatial organisation*: the central dome and four identical porticoes radiate from a square core, making proportion govern *circulation and siting*, not just elevation. A wrong answer ("both use columns") misses the shift from *surface* to *volume* in Vitruvian application.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Palladio's *I Quattro Libri dell'Architettura* (1570) made Vitruvius obsolete for Renaissance architects."
questions.a: Correct: False. Palladio *translated* Vitruvius into a practical pattern book—adding measured drawings of Roman ruins, his own villas, and clear rules for the five orders—making Vitruvian principles *accessible* to builders across Europe. He didn't replace Vitruvius; he operationalised him. A wrong answer ("True, Palladio was better") reveals a misunderstanding of textual transmission: Palladio cites Vitruvius 100+ times; his authority *derives* from Vitruvius.

questions.q: Design a 150-word museum label for a 1550 edition of *De Architectura* that explains to a Class 11 student why this "old book" changed how buildings look today.
questions.a: Expected: Label must mention (1) 1414 rediscovery, (2) the triad *firmitas/utilitas/venustas*, (3) modular proportion linking human body to building (Vitruvian Man), (4) treatises by Alberti/Palladio as mediators, (5) legacy in government buildings, banks, universities worldwide. Poor answer lists dates without explaining *conceptual* impact—shows student sees history as timeline, not idea-flow.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how the rediscovery of Vitruvius provided a theoretical framework that transformed Renaissance architecture from mere imitation of ruins into a principled design system, and can trace this influence through at least three key architects (Brunelleschi, Alberti, Palladio) and their treatises/buildings.
